items.stem:
Read the following extract from an original film script.

EXT. MUMBAI ROOFTOP – NIGHT
Rain lashes the concrete. Neon signs bleed colour into puddles.
CLOSE-UP: ARJUN (16), soaked, clutching a crumpled acceptance letter.
WIDE SHOT: the city stretches to the horizon; Arjun is tiny at the edge of the roof.
SOUND: traffic below fades. Only rain. Then – his phone buzzes.
INSERT – PHONE SCREEN: "Dad: Come home. We'll talk."
Arjun looks at the letter, then at the city. Slowly, he folds the letter into his pocket.
CUT TO BLACK.

The words "WIDE SHOT: the city stretches to the horizon; Arjun is tiny" are an example of which technique?
items.answer: wide shot
items.markingKey: B. "WIDE SHOT: the city stretches to the horizon; Arjun is tiny" is an example of wide shot: the contrast in scale shows his isolation and the size of his decision.

items.stem: Explain why annotating both texts for the same features helps comparison.
items.answer: Looking for the same features (tone, imagery, structure) in both makes it easy to see similarities and differences.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Looking for the same features (tone, imagery, structure) in both makes it easy to see similarities and differences. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Text A: opening of a Gothic short story.

Blackwater Hall had been empty for forty years, yet every night a candle burned in the highest window.
I arrived in November, when the trees had given up their leaves and the fog lay on the moor like a shroud. The gates groaned open before I touched them.
Inside, the air was colder than the night. Portraits lined the staircase – generations of pale Blackwaters – and every pair of painted eyes was turned, I swear, towards the door.
Towards me.

Text B: extract from a Gothic short story told by a teenage narrator.

My brother says I imagine things. He's probably right. I imagined the scratching behind the wallpaper. I imagined that the mirror in the hall shows the room as it was a hundred years ago – the gas lamps, the dark curtains, the woman in grey.
Last night I imagined she turned round.
This morning there were wet footprints on the stairs. Small ones. Bare.
My brother says I must have walked in my sleep. I didn't tell him that my feet were dry.

Using a comparative connective, write two sentences that compare how the two texts approach their shared subject.
items.answer: For example: "Similarly, both use a first-person narrator in an old house where familiar objects (portraits, a mirror) behave impossibly." and "However, Text A builds fear through dramatic Gothic description, whereas Text B uses a calm, self-doubting narrator and a quiet twist."
items.markingKey: For example: "Similarly, both use a first-person narrator in an old house where familiar objects (portraits, a mirror) behave impossibly." and "However, Text A builds fear through dramatic Gothic description, whereas Text B uses a calm, self-doubting narrator and a quiet twist." One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem:
Read the following poem by a student poet, "My Grandmother's Hands".

Her hands are maps of seventy years,
rivers of blue beneath brown paper skin.
They knead the dough like they are
pressing out the war, the boat, the cold.
Flour rises like snow in reverse.
When she holds mine, I feel the journey –
every border folded into her palms.

How does the final line "every border folded into her palms" shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The final line "every border folded into her palms": it extends the map metaphor from the opening, giving the poem a circular shape and a powerful closing image.
items.markingKey: The final line "every border folded into her palms": it extends the map metaphor from the opening, giving the poem a circular shape and a powerful closing image. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Write three annotations comparing the openings of the Gothic house extract and the mirror story.
items.answer: E.g. both first person; A uses dramatic setting (fog "like a shroud"), B uses a casual voice ("He's probably right"); both end on a chilling short line. Credit comparative links.
items.markingKey: E.g. both first person; A uses dramatic setting (fog "like a shroud"), B uses a casual voice ("He's probably right"); both end on a chilling short line. Credit comparative links.

items.answer: Select the most significant features linked to the question; over-annotating wastes time and hides key points.
items.markingKey: Select the most significant features linked to the question; over-annotating wastes time and hides key points. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Planning time in a comparison task is wasted time."
items.answer: Brief, focused planning improves organisation (criterion B) and usually saves time overall.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: writing time is limited; some students think better while writing. Arguments against: planning ensures balanced, organised comparison; it prevents running out of points. Supported judgement: Brief, focused planning improves organisation (criterion B) and usually saves time overall.

items.stem:
Text A: opening of "The Soldier" by Rupert Brooke (1914).

If I should die, think only this of me:
That there's some corner of a foreign field
That is for ever England. There shall be
In that rich earth a richer dust concealed;

Text B: opening of "Anthem for Doomed Youth" by Wilfred Owen (1917).

What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
— Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.

Compare how the two sonnets present death in war. First list three annotations for each text, then write a comparative paragraph.
items.answer: Both are sonnets, but they use the form differently. Text A (Brooke, 1914) idealises death: the euphemism "If I should die" and the metaphor of a "corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England" make death noble and peaceful. Text B (Owen, 1917) protests: the simile "die as cattle" and the onomatopoeic "stuttering rifles' rapid rattle" show anonymous, undignified slaughter. Brooke wrote before the trenches; Owen wrote from experience. Brooke's calm, patriotic tone contrasts with Owen's anger and grief.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both are sonnets, but they use the form differently. Text A (Brooke, 1914) idealises death: the euphemism "If I should die" and the metaphor of a "corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England" make death noble and peaceful. Text B (Owen, 1917) protests: the simile "die as cattle" and the onomatopoeic "stuttering rifles' rapid rattle" show anonymous, undignified slaughter. Brooke wrote before the trenches; Owen wrote from experience. Brooke's calm, patriotic tone contrasts with Owen's anger and grief. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

items.stem:
Text A: travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Text B: diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Using a comparative connective, write two sentences that compare how the two texts approach their shared subject.
items.answer: For example: "Similarly, both writers use humour and vivid similes to describe nature – "like the earth was exhaling" and "like a crown"." and "However, Text A is written for public followers (handle, emoji, comments), while Text B is a private diary that records the writer's honest feelings."
items.markingKey: For example: "Similarly, both writers use humour and vivid similes to describe nature – "like the earth was exhaling" and "like a crown"." and "However, Text A is written for public followers (handle, emoji, comments), while Text B is a private diary that records the writer's honest feelings." One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem: Distinguish between annotating and summarising.
items.answer: Annotating identifies features and their effects in the text; summarising restates the main content in your own words.
items.markingKey: Annotating identifies features and their effects in the text; summarising restates the main content in your own words. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following opening of "Who's for the Game?" by Jessie Pope (1915).

Who's for the game, the biggest that's played,
The red crashing game of a fight?
Who'll grip and tackle the job unafraid?
And who thinks he'd rather sit tight?

Analyse the effect of the bouncy, regular rhythm and rhyme (played/unafraid; fight/tight) in the text.
items.answer: The bouncy, regular rhythm and rhyme (played/unafraid; fight/tight): the jaunty, song-like form makes war sound cheerful and easy to remember.
items.markingKey: The bouncy, regular rhythm and rhyme (played/unafraid; fight/tight): the jaunty, song-like form makes war sound cheerful and easy to remember. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.answer: Indicative content: annotations on both texts; thesis linking them; three points of comparison each with evidence from both texts. Criteria A and B.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: annotations on both texts; thesis linking them; three points of comparison each with evidence from both texts. Criteria A and B.

items.answer: Likewise

items.stem:
Text A: extract from a science-fiction short story.

In 2087 you could sell your memories. Most people sold the boring ones first – queues, commutes, tax forms. The MemoryBank paid well for those; rich people used them to feel ordinary.
Lin sold her seventh birthday to pay the rent.
Afterwards she found a photo of herself in a paper crown, laughing, and felt nothing at all. Not sadness. Not even curiosity.
That was the part the advertisements never mentioned: you didn't miss what you sold. You just became a little less.

Text B: extract from a science-fiction story set on Mars.

The first child born on Mars turned twelve today. Her name is Hope, which everyone agrees was a bit much.
She has never felt rain. She has never seen a dog. When she watches old Earth films, she asks why people walk outside without helmets, as if it were the most dangerous thing in the world.
Tonight she stood at the dome window and pointed at a small blue dot. "Is that really where we're from?" she asked.
Nobody knew how to tell her that it was no longer safe to go back.

Using a comparative connective, write two sentences that compare how the two texts approach their shared subject.
items.answer: For example: "Similarly, both use a futuristic setting and a final line that reveals a hidden cost of the future." and "However, Text A explores inequality through a technology that sells memories, whereas Text B explores environmental loss through a child who cannot return to Earth."
items.markingKey: For example: "Similarly, both use a futuristic setting and a final line that reveals a hidden cost of the future." and "However, Text A explores inequality through a technology that sells memories, whereas Text B explores environmental loss through a child who cannot return to Earth." One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem: Organise these points into a point-by-point plan: tone of both poems; imagery in both poems; form of both poems.
items.answer: Para 1: tone – Pope jaunty vs Owen bitter; Para 2: imagery – game metaphor vs degrading similes; Para 3: form – bouncing rhyme vs heavy rhythm and caesuras.
items.markingKey: Para 1: tone – Pope jaunty vs Owen bitter; Para 2: imagery – game metaphor vs degrading similes; Para 3: form – bouncing rhyme vs heavy rhythm and caesuras.

How does the script use camera and sound to present Arjun's situation? Write a topic sentence for a comparative paragraph that could link this text to another text you know on a similar theme.
items.answer: The close-up on the crumpled acceptance letter tells us it is central, while the wide shot shrinks Arjun against the city, showing isolation. Sound narrows from traffic to rain, so the phone's buzz is startling; the insert shot reveals the father's message. Mise-en-scène (rain, neon "bleeding" into puddles, the roof's edge) creates a melancholy, tense mood, and the cut to black leaves his choice unresolved.

items.stem:
Text A: extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

Text B: speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

Compare how the two texts present the importance of real connection between young people. Use a point-by-point structure and at least four different comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both texts value face-to-face connection. Text A dramatises it through one moment: Mei's isolation ("Twenty-eight faces turned") ends when Zara offers a seat and a shared interest, and the single word "Yes" marks belonging. Text B argues for it directly: the paradox "Connected, but alone" and the school statistic show loneliness, and anaphoric "Let's..." imperatives call for action. Difference: the novel shows through character and dialogue (implicit), the speech persuades through rhetoric and evidence (explicit); both end on an image of friendship.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both texts value face-to-face connection. Text A dramatises it through one moment: Mei's isolation ("Twenty-eight faces turned") ends when Zara offers a seat and a shared interest, and the single word "Yes" marks belonging. Text B argues for it directly: the paradox "Connected, but alone" and the school statistic show loneliness, and anaphoric "Let's..." imperatives call for action. Difference: the novel shows through character and dialogue (implicit), the speech persuades through rhetoric and evidence (explicit); both end on an image of friendship. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

items.stem:
Read the following opening of "Dulce et Decorum Est" by Wilfred Owen (written 1917, published 1920).

Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs,
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots,
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;

How might a reader in 1915 and a reader today respond differently to this text? Refer to specific details.
items.answer: Protest: Owen presents war from the soldier's point of view as degrading, exhausting and inhuman, directly contradicting the heroic images of propaganda.
items.markingKey: Protest: Owen presents war from the soldier's point of view as degrading, exhausting and inhuman, directly contradicting the heroic images of propaganda. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

Read the following advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.

Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

items.answer: One reader might see a caring solution to loneliness; a more critical reader might find it sad that a machine replaces human visits, and notice the advert implies families "forget birthdays".

items.stem:
Text A: extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Text B: advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

Compare how the two texts present the relationship between people and animals (or animal-like companions). In your answer, comment on the effect each text has on its audience.
items.answer: Text A presents a real, vulnerable dog ("thin ... muddy") whose rescue tests Thabo's kindness; the relationship involves responsibility and moral choice. Text B presents a robot dog as a convenient companion that "never needs a walk", selling comfort through a testimonial and a warm image. Text A uses narrative suspense and symbolism (the "question mark" ear); Text B uses persuasive anaphora and a slogan. A critical comparison: the story values care and effort, while the advert removes effort – raising questions about what companionship means.

Text A uses narrative suspense and symbolism (the "question mark" ear); Text B uses persuasive anaphora and a slogan. A critical comparison: the story values care and effort, while the advert removes effort – raising questions about what companionship means. When the rains came, Mama said the city became honest. 'Lagos cannot hide her potholes under water,' she said, 'and people cannot hide their hearts under umbrellas.'
That evening the road outside our compound turned into a brown river. Mr Adeyemi from next door, who had not spoken to us since the argument about the generator, waded across carrying a sack of rice above his head.
'Your roof is leaking,' he said. 'Mine is not. Come.'
We spent the night in his parlour, two families, one candle, nobody mentioning the generator.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript for young actors.

SCENE 2. A school hall. Night. Rain hammers on the roof. The lights flicker.
ANA: (whispering) Did you hear that?
LUCAS: It's the wind. (He doesn't look up from his phone.)
ANA: The wind doesn't knock three times.
(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)
LUCAS: (forcing a laugh) OK. That's... a very polite wind.
(The lights go out. Blackout.)

Analyse the effect of the contrast between Ana and Lucas in the text.
items.answer: The contrast between Ana and Lucas: Ana's alertness and Lucas's dismissiveness create conflict and let the audience share the shift in Lucas's feelings.

items.stem:
Read the following poem by a student poet, "My Grandmother's Hands".

Her hands are maps of seventy years,
rivers of blue beneath brown paper skin.
They knead the dough like they are
pressing out the war, the boat, the cold.
Flour rises like snow in reverse.
When she holds mine, I feel the journey –
every border folded into her palms.

How does the poet use imagery to present the grandmother and her past? Write a topic sentence for a comparative paragraph that could link this text to another text you know on a similar theme.
items.answer: The extended map metaphor ("maps of seventy years", "every border folded into her palms") presents her hands as a record of a journey across borders. The simile of kneading out "the war, the boat, the cold" shows her quietly working through trauma, while "Flour rises like snow in reverse" softens the past into warmth. The speaker's touch ("When she holds mine") passes the history on.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The extended map metaphor ("maps of seventy years", "every border folded into her palms") presents her hands as a record of a journey across borders. The simile of kneading out "the war, the boat, the cold" shows her quietly working through trauma, while "Flour rises like snow in reverse" softens the past into warmth. The speaker's touch ("When she holds mine") passes the history on. items.stem: ""It makes the reader want to read on" is a strong comment on effect." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It is too general; strong comments explain the specific feeling or thought created and why.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Planning time in a comparison task is wasted time."
items.answer: Brief, focused planning improves organisation (criterion B) and usually saves time overall.

items.stem: "Similarities between texts are less interesting than differences." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Both matter: similarities establish common ground that makes differences significant.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: differences reveal contrasting perspectives; contrast is vivid. Arguments against: similarities can reveal shared methods or contexts; similarities make differences meaningful. items.stem: "A text means whatever the reader feels it means." To what extent is this view justified?

items.answer: comparative connective

items.stem: Distinguish between the actual response and the intended effect.
items.answer: The intended effect is what the writer seems to want readers to feel; the actual response may differ depending on the reader's context and values.

items.stem:
Text A: report of a climate protest (Report A, from a national newspaper).

STUDENTS BRING CITY TO STANDSTILL
Thousands of school pupils skipped lessons on Friday to block the main bridge into the city, causing traffic delays of up to two hours.
Police said three people were arrested for public disorder.
"My son should be in maths, not in the road," said commuter Peter Hale.
Organisers claimed 12,000 attended, though police estimated 5,000.

Text B: report of a climate protest (Report B, from a youth news website).

12,000 YOUNG PEOPLE DEMAND CLIMATE ACTION
Up to 12,000 students marched peacefully across the main bridge on Friday, calling on the government to meet its emissions targets.
"We're missing one day of school. Our future is missing a plan," said organiser Amara Diallo, 16.
Scientists from the city university joined the march.
Police reported three arrests.

Using a comparative connective, write two sentences that compare how the two texts approach their shared subject.
items.answer: For example: "Similarly, both report that a protest took place on the main bridge on Friday and that three people were arrested." and "However, Report A presents the students as disruptive by quoting an annoyed commuter, whereas Report B presents them as peaceful and purposeful by quoting a young organiser."
items.markingKey: For example: "Similarly, both report that a protest took place on the main bridge on Friday and that three people were arrested." and "However, Report A presents the students as disruptive by quoting an annoyed commuter, whereas Report B presents them as peaceful and purposeful by quoting a young organiser." One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem: Distinguish between block structure and point-by-point structure.
items.answer: Point-by-point discusses both texts within each paragraph around a shared point; block structure discusses all of Text A, then all of Text B, with comparison mainly at the end.

items.answer: Annotating identifies features and their effects in the text; summarising restates the main content in your own words.

items.stem:
Text A: opening of "Dulce et Decorum Est" by Wilfred Owen (written 1917, published 1920).

Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs,
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots,
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;

Text B: opening of "Who's for the Game?" by Jessie Pope (1915).

Who's for the game, the biggest that's played,
The red crashing game of a fight?
Who'll grip and tackle the job unafraid?
And who thinks he'd rather sit tight?

Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the two texts, supporting each with a reference to both texts.
items.answer: Similarity: both poems address the experience of young men going to war and try to change how readers think about it. Difference: Text A uses grim similes and a slow rhythm to expose suffering, whereas Text B uses a sporting metaphor and a jaunty rhythm to make war sound exciting.
items.markingKey: Similarity: both poems address the experience of young men going to war and try to change how readers think about it. Difference: Text A uses grim similes and a slow rhythm to expose suffering, whereas Text B uses a sporting metaphor and a jaunty rhythm to make war sound exciting. One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a Gothic short story.

Blackwater Hall had been empty for forty years, yet every night a candle burned in the highest window.
I arrived in November, when the trees had given up their leaves and the fog lay on the moor like a shroud. The gates groaned open before I touched them.
Inside, the air was colder than the night. Portraits lined the staircase – generations of pale Blackwaters – and every pair of painted eyes was turned, I swear, towards the door.
Towards me.

How does the writer create a Gothic atmosphere in this opening? Write a topic sentence for a comparative paragraph that could link this text to another text you know on a similar theme.
items.answer: The writer uses classic Gothic conventions: an isolated, decaying house and a hostile landscape. The simile "like a shroud" links the fog to death, personification ("given up their leaves") creates hopelessness, and supernatural hints (gates opening untouched, portraits' eyes turned to the door) make the familiar uncanny. Structurally the focus narrows from moor to narrator, ending on the isolated "Towards me." to trap the reader in the narrator's fear.

The simile "like a shroud" links the fog to death, personification ("given up their leaves") creates hopelessness, and supernatural hints (gates opening untouched, portraits' eyes turned to the door) make the familiar uncanny. Structurally the focus narrows from moor to narrator, ending on the isolated "Towards me." to trap the reader in the narrator's fear. items.stem:
Text A: advertisement for running shoes, printed in a teen sports magazine.

[Image: a girl sprints up concrete steps at dawn; the city below is still asleep.]
THEY SAID TOO YOUNG. THEY SAID TOO SMALL. THEY SAID TOO LATE.
She said: watch me.
STRIDE X – featherlight foam, grip that never quits.
Your city. Your rules. Your run.
#RunYourWay  |  Available now in 12 colours.

Text B: interview from a teen magazine with a young chef in Lima.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'
Q: What's the hardest part?
A: Waking up at 4 a.m. to buy fish. And being taken seriously. People ask where my parents are.
Q: Advice for other teens?
A: Start small. Burn things. Try again.

Compare how the two texts present young people's determination to succeed.
items.answer: Text A (advert) dramatises determination through anaphora ("THEY SAID TOO YOUNG...") and a defiant reply, using it to sell shoes; Text B (interview) lets a real young chef describe hardships (4 a.m. starts, not being taken seriously) and ends with the tricolon "Start small. Burn things. Try again." Both show young people proving doubters wrong. Difference: the advert's determination is an image constructed for profit; the interview's is grounded in specific detail and modest humour, making it more convincing.

items.stem:
Text A: satirical article from a student humour website.

SCHOOL BANS THINKING TO IMPROVE TEST SCORES
Greenfield Academy has announced a ban on independent thought, after research showed that students who think 'take too long' to fill in multiple-choice answers.
"Curiosity is a distraction," said Head of Results Ms Graves. "Our students don't need to understand. They need to tick."
Questions will now be permitted only on Fridays, between 2:14 and 2:16 p.m.
Parents have welcomed the news. "My son used to ask 'Why?' all the time," said one father. "Now he just says 'Which box?'"

Text B: parody advertisement from a student magazine.

[Image: a glossy bottle labelled PERFECT™ on a pink background with sparkles.]
TIRED OF BEING YOURSELF?
Introducing PERFECT™ – the filter you can drink!
✓ Removes freckles, opinions and personality
✓ Makes you look exactly like everyone else on your feed
✓ Side effects may include: loss of self, endless scrolling, and spending all your money
Because you're worth nothing... until you're PERFECT™.

Compare how the two texts use humour to criticise aspects of young people's lives. Begin with a comparative thesis.
items.answer: Both are satirical: they imitate a genre (a news report; a beauty advert) and exaggerate it to expose a target – exam culture and beauty/social-media culture. Text A uses deadpan irony ("Curiosity is a distraction"), absurd precision (2:14–2:16 p.m.) and a telling name (Ms Graves). Text B uses an ironic benefit list ("Removes freckles, opinions and personality") and a twisted slogan. Text A targets institutions; Text B targets the media industry that sells insecurity.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from the Prologue of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare (c. 1595).

CHORUS:
Two households, both alike in dignity,
In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;

How does "star-cross'd lovers" shape the reader's response to the text?
items.answer: Compound adjective / imagery of fate: "star-cross'd lovers" – it suggests the stars (fate) are against the lovers, foreshadowing tragedy.
